posts.title: When Did tmux Overtake Screen?
posts.description: tmux gained ground in developer workflows during the early to mid-2010s. The history explains the shift, but does not establish a global usage crossover.

blocks.text: The early to mid-2010s is the best window for the shift toward tmux in developer workflows. That is a reading of the historical record, not a measured date when tmux passed GNU Screen in total users. The sources show a new project in 2007, operating system adoption in 2009, and an established culture of tmux tutorials and migration guides by 2012–2015.

If you remember Screen being the obvious answer and then finding tmux in everyone’s dotfiles, there was no single release that marked the handoff. Different teams switched at different times. A developer configuring a new laptop and an administrator reconnecting to an old server had different reasons to change.
2007–2009: tmux becomes a credible alternative

Nicholas Marriott published the first version of tmux in late 2007. In a 2009 interview, he described having been a heavy Screen user who wanted a more extensible codebase and a different interface. One specific goal was sharing a window between terminals while keeping other windows separate. By then, he considered both programs usable enough that people could move between them without losing too many features.

OpenBSD 4.6 shipped on October 18, 2009, with tmux in its base system. The release notes identify it as the replacement for window(1). This was an important distribution milestone, but it was not an announcement that tmux had displaced Screen among Unix users.
2012–2015: evidence of a change in everyday use

By March 2012, thoughtbot was publishing instructions for getting tmux copy and paste working on Mac OS X. A guide about an integration problem tells us something different from a project announcement: people were already trying to fit tmux into their daily development environment.

A February 2015 migration account gives a more direct glimpse of the shift. Tom Wey wrote that he had been the sole Screen user at New Bamboo, surrounded by enthusiastic tmux users. Access to that shared expertise was his biggest reason for switching. This is evidence from one workplace, not a representative survey, but it captures how a tool becomes the local default.

source.label: Tom Wey’s account of switching from Screen.

blocks.text: Those examples support describing the early to mid-2010s as a transition period in developer communities. They do not justify picking 2013, or any other year, as the moment a worldwide user count crossed. Establishing that would require comparable usage measurements over time.
Why tmux appealed to Screen users

Marriott’s 2011 design paper explains the appeal beyond the visible panes. tmux was built around a server managing windows, a consistent command interface, and shell scripting. Commands used from a key binding could also be used from the shell. The design made repeatable terminal workspaces a natural use case.

Consider a project with an editor, a test runner, and a log window. Being able to create and arrange that workspace with commands saves repeated setup. Once a teammate shares a useful configuration, the next person has less to learn from scratch. The migration account above suggests that this exchange of knowledge mattered alongside the software’s features.

blocks.alt: Two terminal clients connect to a server holding a workspace with three panes.
blocks.text: Conceptual illustration: a shared terminal workspace that persists between connections.

Screen’s capabilities also deserve a fair account. Vertical splitting was already available in its development version in February 2007. Its current manual documents horizontal and vertical splits, plus layouts that preserve arrangements across detach and reattach. Claims that Screen simply cannot split a terminal confuse particular versions or configurations with the program as a whole.

The distinction is in how the tools organize that work and how comfortable their interfaces feel to the person using them. Screen’s layout support provides another way to retain a working arrangement, so persistent layouts alone cannot explain every migration.
What would count as overtaking?

Installed packages, active users, search interest, and tutorial volume measure different things. A package can be installed without being used. Search traffic can come from troubleshooting. GitHub stars measure attention on one hosting platform. A comparison using the bare word “screen” also needs to separate the terminal multiplexer from unrelated searches.

For a history of developer habits, I would place the shift in the early to mid-2010s and keep that qualification attached. For a claim about total usage, the evidence here does not establish a crossover. Screen users did not need to stop working for tmux to become the tool their colleagues reached for first.

hero.alt: Older and newer terminal workstations with split panes and overlapping terminal windows.
hero.text: Conceptual illustration: changing terminal habits across generations of workstations.

posts.title: Flock Cameras in Los Angeles: Privacy Risks
posts.description: What Los Angeles’s license plate cameras collect, who can search the records, and what the LAPD audit found about privacy and oversight.

blocks.text: A license plate camera records more than a number. It records where a vehicle was and when it passed. Across Los Angeles, police have added that capability to roadside cameras and equipment already inside patrol cars. I find the scale alarming because the records can outlast the trip, while rules about who can search them have lagged behind deployment.

Flock Safety sells some of these systems. Automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, also come from other vendors. Switching brands does not necessarily stop collection. To understand what a local program does, look at the cameras, the databases they feed, and the people allowed to search those records.
Flock cameras and LAPD’s wider ALPR system

The LAPD inspector general’s July 2026 review describes how quickly capacity can grow without new poles on the street. In 2023, the department activated plate recognition in about 1,500 police vehicles. It later received a loan of 50 Flock cameras for the Pacific Palisades area after the January 2025 fire.

The review counted more than 210 million plate reads in August and September 2025. A vehicle can appear many times, so that figure does not count unique cars or people. The report also found gaps in agreements covering data security and access. Collection was already running at scale while those terms remained unresolved.

Nearby cities operate separate programs. La Cañada Flintridge’s fixed Flock cameras are run by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department. The city says its data is shared only with authorized California law enforcement agencies. Its policy does not describe every system in the county, and LAPD’s decisions do not switch those cameras off.

By October, Council District 13 reported that no Flock cameras were transmitting to LAPD and that sharing with outside agencies had stopped. It also reported that more than 4,000 officers could search ALPR records, without regular reviews of who still needed access. That leaves a large group of users whose permissions need scrutiny.

The records reviewed here do not establish a monthly growth rate for every ALPR across Los Angeles County. A purchased camera may be inactive. A patrol car may gain plate recognition through a software change. These differences matter when comparing counts or claiming that surveillance has stopped.

blocks.alt: A car’s license plate sightings become records in a filing cabinet with connections to other archives.
blocks.text: A sighting becomes a searchable record. Conceptual AI-generated illustration for aaronkaufman.com.
Why stored plate sightings create privacy risks

A series of sightings can suggest visits to a clinic, a place of worship, a workplace, or a protest. That is a risk even without facial recognition. The data can reveal sensitive associations, but it cannot establish who was driving or why the car was there. Investigators need to keep those limits in view.

The audit shows both useful results and reasons for caution. It linked 337 alerts to stolen vehicle recoveries. It also identified 161 alerts where officers confirmed the plate match but later found the vehicle was not stolen. Those findings describe alert outcomes, not a measured error rate for every camera or search. A fair assessment should also separate live alerts from later database searches. They serve different purposes and need different measures of success.

Flock announced changes in August, including a shorter standard retention period and mandatory audit measures. The Associated Press reported that some requirements were due by January 1, 2027. Officials should verify which settings are active locally, who can override them, and what happens to data saved under an exception.

source.label: Associated Press report on the announced safeguards.

blocks.text: What Los Angeles residents should ask for

I would start with a public inventory of active cameras, software features, and outside data sources. Each program should name its operator and publish its cost, contract, privacy policy, and renewal date. A list of hardware alone will miss access to records collected somewhere else.

Access should follow a person’s current job. Remove accounts when staff leave or change roles. Require a case number and a stated reason for each search, with any emergency override recorded for review. Keep logs that show who searched, what they requested, and whether they exported the results.

Logs need someone to read them. An independent reviewer should check a sample of searches against the cases cited, investigate unusual patterns, and publish findings. A system that records every query can still permit abuse if nobody examines the record or acts on it.

Set short deletion periods and spell out when evidence may be kept longer. Check whether deletion reaches exports and copies held by other agencies. Residents can ask their council offices for those rules and the latest audit. A claim that data is deleted needs evidence from the systems that hold it.

Expansion should require another public decision, including when equipment is donated or a software update adds new tracking features. Temporary deployments need expiration dates. Publish the results, costs, and misuse findings before renewal. Los Angeles should decide how much vehicle history police may collect and search before granting the next extension.

hero.alt: Editorial illustration of license plate cameras watching cars on a palm-lined Los Angeles street.
hero.text: Original AI-generated illustration for aaronkaufman.com. Conceptual scene, not a map of installed cameras.

posts.title: Ed25519, Quantum Resistance, and AI
posts.description: Ed25519 is not quantum-resistant. Understand what AI changes, how post-quantum signatures differ, and how to plan a migration.

blocks.text: Ed25519 is useful, widely deployed, and not quantum-resistant. AI does not change that answer. What it changes is the environment around the signature: more generated code, more automated decisions, and new opportunities to mishandle the keys that make authentication work. Planning for quantum attacks means replacing vulnerable cryptography while keeping those everyday failures in view.
What Ed25519 signatures guarantee

Ed25519 is a digital signature scheme. A private key signs a message, and the corresponding public key lets someone verify it. Its public keys are 32 bytes and its signatures are 64 bytes. RFC 8032 describes an intended classical security level of about 128 bits. Those properties make it useful where small keys and signatures matter.

A valid signature establishes a relationship between specific data and a signing key. Trust in a person or organization also depends on how that public key was obtained. If an attacker replaces both a download and the public key offered beside it, checking the signature against that replacement key provides no useful assurance about the original publisher.

Signing also does not encrypt the message. Nor does it prove that signed code is safe, a model is accurate, or a document is truthful. A publisher can sign a bad release. An attacker who steals its signing key can produce signatures that verify correctly.
Why quantum computers change the calculation

Ed25519 relies on an elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could solve that problem and derive the signing secret from a public key, allowing forged signatures. Switching to a larger conventional elliptic curve does not remove that class of attack. RFC 8032 explicitly identifies both Ed25519 and Ed448 as vulnerable to quantum computing.

That requires a cryptographically relevant quantum computer, not simply a machine advertised as quantum. AI assistance does not supply the quantum hardware this attack requires. The engineering problem is to prepare systems that may remain in service for years without treating an uncertain arrival date as an excuse to postpone every migration decision.

Signatures also face a different timing problem from encrypted traffic collected for later decryption. With signatures, the concern is future forgery and whether verifiers can distinguish legitimate historical records from newly forged ones. Software updates, archived documents, and trust anchors can need protection long after their original signing date.
Where AI creates immediate risk

The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre assesses that AI will make parts of cyber intrusion more efficient and effective. For an operator, that is a reason to examine exposed services, credentials, and release systems. An attacker may gain more from compromising a build job or tricking a maintainer than from attacking the signature algorithm itself.

Consider an AI agent preparing a software release. If it can modify source code, approve the build, and invoke the signing service, the signature may authenticate a release nobody independently checked. That is an authorization failure. Changing Ed25519 to a quantum-resistant algorithm would still leave the agent with the same excessive authority.

Separate generation from approval. Give signing services narrow permissions, log their use, and require review before sensitive releases. When signing model artifacts, define which weights, configuration, tokenizer, and dependencies the signature covers. Verifying one file does not establish the integrity of every component loaded alongside it.

blocks.alt: An automated arm prepares a document, a human opens an approval gate, and a separate machine signs the release.
blocks.text: Keep generation, approval, and signing separate. Conceptual AI-generated illustration for aaronkaufman.com.
Moving to quantum-resistant signatures

NIST standardized ML-DSA in FIPS 204 and SLH-DSA in FIPS 205 in 2024. They use different foundations: structured lattices for ML-DSA and hash functions for SLH-DSA. Both are intended to resist known quantum attacks. They still require sound implementations, protected keys, and ongoing cryptanalysis. Quantum-resistant describes a security goal, not a promise that software cannot fail.
ML-KEM serves a different purpose. It establishes a shared secret for uses such as encryption. It does not replace an Ed25519 signature.

The same distinction matters in SSH. OpenSSH supports post-quantum key agreement, but that does not automatically make an Ed25519 authentication key quantum-resistant. Check the negotiated key agreement and the signature algorithms separately. A product’s quantum security claim may cover one part of the connection.

Start by inventorying where signatures are created and verified. Include release tooling, firmware, package repositories, and devices that cannot easily be updated. Test supported migration paths with real clients. Measure larger signatures, storage limits, verification costs, and failure handling before changing production trust rules.

Plan how new public keys reach verifiers before changing the signer. Test missing signatures, altered artifacts, expired credentials, and attempts to select an older algorithm. Make rollback rules explicit so a failed upgrade cannot quietly restore a retired trust path. Keep an owner responsible for each stage of the transition.

If a protocol combines classical and post-quantum signatures, understand its acceptance rules. Requiring both signatures can preserve protection when one scheme fails. Accepting either can preserve the weaker path. Use reviewed protocol designs rather than inventing a combination that merely attaches two signatures.

Ed25519 deserves a migration plan based on its limits. AI makes disciplined access control and release review more urgent. Quantum computing makes the choice of signature algorithm a long term concern. Treat both as engineering work with named owners, tested changes, and a way to verify progress.

hero.alt: A signing machine marks a document, with a stylized quantum computer in the distance.
hero.text: Digital signatures and quantum computing. Conceptual AI-generated illustration for aaronkaufman.com.

posts.title: The State of Email in 2026: Privacy and PGP
posts.description: I left Gmail in 2019 and eventually settled on StartMail. I want reliable email, PGP, and the freedom to choose my own client.

blocks.text: I finished removing Google from my life in 2019. Gmail was the last holdout. Email is a miserable thing to move because your address becomes attached to everything, including accounts you forgot existed until they send a password reset.

I bounced between providers before settling on StartMail. My requirements were straightforward: IMAP, SMTP, and PGP. I self-host my calendar over CalDAV. I want to choose the programs that handle those jobs without asking a mail company which operating systems I am allowed to like.
For private email in 2026, I want a mailbox I can use with my own software. Here is how Gmail, Proton Mail, Tuta, Fastmail, and StartMail measure up against that requirement.
Gmail in 2026: advertising, AI, and email privacy

“You are the product” describes my problem with advertising-funded email. Companies profit from access to your attention, with personal information helping target the pitch. Google says Gmail ads are not based on scanning your messages and that it does not sell your personal information. Selling advertisers access to an audience is still monetization. I would rather pay for a mailbox than participate in that arrangement.

This year's Gemini Personal Intelligence pitch connects Gmail with other Google services to personalize assistance. Those connections are opt-in and off by default. Google says it does not train directly on your inbox. I still do not want AI reading my email to personalize an answer. My receipts do not need a relationship with a chatbot.

Gmail still supports third-party clients through IMAP. My objection is the dependency surrounding the mailbox. I left Google because I wanted less of Google in my life. Seven years later, connecting more Google products is a lousy invitation back.
Outlook and iCloud Mail: who can access your email?

Switching providers while overlooking the client can undermine the whole exercise. Microsoft's Outlook cloud-sync feature copies mail from connected accounts into Microsoft data centers. Supported accounts and platforms vary. That is another company handling the mailbox, even when the address belongs to an independent provider. Read what the client does before giving it credentials.

Apple's privacy reputation does not make iCloud Mail end-to-end encrypted. Mail remains outside that protection even with Advanced Data Protection enabled. Apple documents this. Read the per-service details instead of assuming a company's strongest privacy feature covers every product wearing its logo.
KISS: keep it simple, stupid

IMAP gives clients access to a mailbox. SMTP handles sending. Neither is glamorous, and neither needs a launch event. Their value is that the interface survives a change of software. I can dislike a mail client, replace it, and keep receiving mail at the same address.

No bells and whistles. Receive mail, send mail, and let me choose the client. I want fewer dependencies and less software between me and a message. KISS still leaves room for strong authentication, encryption, and updates. It does not require an AI assistant, a bundled workspace, or another dashboard to babysit.

Open protocols alone do not prevent lock-in. Your address, stored messages, contacts, and recovery arrangements can still make leaving painful. A domain you control helps preserve the address. Exportable mail and tested backups help preserve the history. An exit should be something you can execute, not a reassuring sentence on a pricing page.
Private email in 2026: Proton, Tuta, and Fastmail
Proton Mail: Bridge and reliability concerns
Proton Mail supports OpenPGP exchanges with people outside Proton. That interoperability matters. I do not want everyone I email to need an account with my provider.

Its Bridge application supplies local IMAP/SMTP access for desktop clients. It requires a paid plan and supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, not mobile. That is another process to maintain. I prefer direct server access.

Reliability concerns me more. Proton's August 27, 2026 outage followed a datacenter cooling failure. Its own report describes lost redundancy, database failover complications, and resilience improvements still underway. Those are major operational problems for a service people depend on for mail.

Further disruption followed on September 1 during recovery-related maintenance. Proton reported instability under load and reduced capacity, then said service was restored without lost data. That is enough to make reliability a deciding factor for me.

Meanwhile, Proton's product announcements include video meetings and an AI assistant. From the outside, it feels like too many pots on the stove. I cannot see how its teams divide their time. For email, I care more about a quiet incident log than another launch.
Tuta: no IMAP or OpenPGP support
Tuta uses its own encryption system and clients, with no IMAP or PGP support. It encrypts subjects too, but fails my interoperability requirements.

My default rule is “never roll your own crypto.” TutaCrypt is a custom protocol built from established components, including X25519 and Kyber. That is different from inventing a cipher. A new protocol still needs expert scrutiny of how those components fit together. I prefer OpenPGP compatibility and encryption I can use across providers.
Fastmail: IMAP, SMTP, and PGP in your client

Fastmail is closer to the conventional model I want. It supports IMAP, SMTP, CalDAV, and CardDAV on eligible plans. Its Basic plan excludes those interfaces, so check the plan before paying. A standards-based service still needs the right subscription attached to it.

Fastmail does not provide an end-to-end encrypted mailbox by default. Its servers process message content for features such as search. You can use PGP in a compatible client, with the associated key management left to you. That is an intelligible tradeoff, provided you understand what the provider can read.
Encrypted email: TLS vs. end-to-end encryption

“Encrypted email” needs a follow-up question. TLS protects the connection to the server. Encryption at rest protects stored data under a particular key-management arrangement. Neither, by itself, means only the sender and recipient can read the message. I want to know where plaintext exists and who can obtain the keys. A padlock icon has never been an adequate architecture diagram.

source.label: Fastmail's explanation of transport and message encryption

blocks.text: Why I chose StartMail for private email

StartMail gives me direct IMAP and SMTP access with separate device credentials. That fits how I want email to work. I can choose a client around my operating system and habits instead of arranging my habits around the provider's application.

StartMail also has mobile apps now. Fine. An optional app can be useful. My objection starts when the app becomes the admission ticket and my existing client becomes somebody else's deprecated use case.

The PGP distinction needs spelling out. StartMail's built-in webmail cryptography runs on its servers. Handling OpenPGP yourself in a local client is a different arrangement, with different trust assumptions. A PGP feature does not automatically mean the provider never handles decrypted content or key material. Decide where encryption happens before deciding what it protects.

blocks.alt: An envelope with protected contents, an exposed address label, and a separate key.
blocks.text: Conceptual illustration: protecting message contents does not conceal every part of delivery.

PGP is a requirement for me, not a claim that every message I send is encrypted. The recipient needs a compatible setup. Keys need verification and backups. Routing information remains visible, and a compromised endpoint can expose a message after decryption. None of that makes PGP pointless. It makes knowing its limits part of using it.
Quantum resistance raises a separate set of questions. I cover the limits of today's digital signatures and the move to post-quantum alternatives in
StartMail calendars and self-hosted CalDAV

StartMail says it does not currently offer a calendar. My CalDAV server is separate and self-hosted, not a StartMail feature. That suits me. Changing email providers should not require moving every appointment along with the mailbox.

blocks.alt: Separate mail, calendar, and contact tools connected to a computer through detachable cables.
blocks.text: Conceptual illustration: independent services connected through replaceable interfaces.

Self-hosting comes with maintenance, backups, updates, and recovery. I accept that work for my calendar. Paying someone else to operate my mailbox is a separate decision. KISS includes knowing which jobs I want to maintain.

StartMail is where I landed. My requirements remain IMAP, SMTP, PGP, and enough separation to change my mind later. Deliver the mail, let me read it in my own client, and leave the rest of my life out of the sales pitch.

hero.alt: An independent mailbox connects to several mail clients beside a closed software kiosk.
hero.text: Conceptual illustration: choosing a mail client independently of the provider.

posts.title: Emacs vs Vim: How the Editor War Started
posts.description: When did the Emacs vs Vim rivalry start? Trace its roots in 1970s Emacs and vi, the 1980s editor wars, and Vim’s arrival in 1991.

blocks.text: The Emacs vs Vim rivalry grew out of the older Emacs vs vi debate. Its roots reach back to the editors developed during the 1970s, and it was an established argument in Unix circles by the mid-1980s. Vim entered the story with its first public release on November 2, 1991. There is no well-established date for the first argument, and the two original editors appearing around the same period does not mean their users immediately declared war.

The distinction matters when tracing the rivalry through history. People remember the dispute under the names they use today. But Bill Joy's vi and Bram Moolenaar's Vim are different programs, separated by years of development. The rivalry had already acquired its competing habits, technical complaints, and jokes before Vim gave one side a new standard bearer.
The 1970s origins of Emacs and vi

Emacs emerged at MIT from work on TECO, an earlier editor whose commands could be assembled into macros. Richard Stallman's account dates the first operational EMACS system to late 1976. Guy Steele and other MIT programmers contributed to the editing systems and ideas from which it developed. Users could extend the editor instead of accepting a fixed collection of commands.

source.label: Stallman’s history of the original Emacs.

blocks.text: The original Emacs ran on a PDP-10 under MIT's Incompatible Timesharing System. It was not the GNU Emacs people usually mean today. Keeping those implementations separate matters, because otherwise the story incorrectly places modern Emacs Lisp and the GNU project in the original editor's beginnings.

At Berkeley, Bill Joy developed vi through work on ex, a Unix line editor. Its name came from the visual interface that let users work across a terminal screen. In a 1984 interview, Joy recalled designing the screen editor after Berkeley acquired ADM-3A terminals. He placed that work around the 1976 presidential election. The available hardware helped determine what he built.

source.label: Bill Joy’s 1984 Unix Review interview, reproduced.

blocks.text: Those origins produced different expectations about editing. Emacs encouraged users to extend a working environment. Vi offered a compact command language for manipulating text. Neither description captures everything either editor could do, but the contrast gave their advocates something substantial to argue about.
How editing preferences became an editor war

The most visible disagreement concerned modes. In vi, ordinary letters can be editing commands. Pressing i enters insert mode, where typing adds text. Escape returns to command mode. A beginner who forgets the current mode can issue commands while trying to write a sentence. An experienced user can make substantial changes with very little typing.

Emacs normally inserts ordinary characters directly and assigns many commands to combinations involving Control or Meta. It also has modes, but its major and minor modes usually configure behavior for a task or file type. That is a different meaning from vi's distinction between entering text and issuing commands. Calling Emacs simply modeless hides this difference.

source.label: GNU Emacs manual: major and minor modes.

blocks.text: Consider deleting several words. A vi user learns to combine an operation with a movement and a count. An Emacs user learns commands that can be repeated, rebound, or extended. Both approaches reward practice. After enough repetition, changing editors means interrupting movements that previously required almost no conscious attention.

blocks.alt: Lavender and orange groups of keyboard keys connect to the same text on a terminal screen.
blocks.text: Different keyboard habits can accomplish the same editing task. Conceptual AI-generated illustration.
That helps explain the intensity, though it cannot establish the date of any particular quarrel.

An editor sits between a programmer and nearly every line of work. Criticism of the tool can sound like criticism of the hours spent learning it. Add different machines, different workloads, and different local teaching habits, and personal preference starts looking like universal truth.
By the 1980s, the argument had become folklore

Evidence from the period is more useful than a tidy origin legend. The book Life with UNIX records a deliberately insulting title for a 1985 European UNIX User Group debate about vi. That gives us a dated example of public editor antagonism. It does not identify the first hostile conversation or prove that a single event launched the rivalry.

GNU Emacs also appeared in 1985, bringing Stallman's newer implementation into the same Unix world where vi was already familiar. Discussions on networked forums helped users encounter opposing preferences beyond their own computer rooms. Arguments about memory use, keyboard commands, customization, and availability were easy to repeat because each reflected a problem somebody had personally experienced.

The religious language made the dispute memorable. Stallman's Saint IGNUcius routine turned devotion to Emacs into an explicit joke, complete with a halo. His explanation also says that using a free version of vi is no sin. That detail gets lost when the performance is treated as evidence of an absolute technical or moral prohibition.

Joy himself was less doctrinaire than the rivalry suggests. In that interview, he praised Emacs for its programmability and said he had enjoyed using it. His frustration was maintaining his own extensions as the software changed. That is a recognizable complaint about upkeep, even from the author of vi. It makes the history more interesting than a contest between two irreconcilable camps.

source.label: Joy on Emacs and maintaining extensions.

blocks.text: When Vim joined the rivalry in 1991

Bram Moolenaar wanted a usable vi-style editor on his Amiga. In his own history of Vim, he describes improving an existing clone because the available alternatives did not satisfy him. The first public release, Vim 1.14, appeared on Fred Fish disk 591 on November 2, 1991. A Unix port followed in 1992.

source.label: Bram Moolenaar’s account of Vim’s history.

blocks.alt: An Amiga-style keyboard computer, CRT display, and floppy disk evoke Vim’s first public release in 1991.
blocks.text: Vim first reached the public on an Amiga software disk in 1991. Conceptual AI-generated illustration, not archival hardware documentation.

Vim initially meant Vi IMitation and later became Vi IMproved. Features such as multiple levels of undo, multiple windows, and eventually syntax highlighting expanded what users could do while preserving familiar editing commands. It gave people who liked vi's interaction model reasons to keep using that model on newer systems.

source.label: Moolenaar on Vim’s name and added features.

blocks.text: This also weakened the old stereotype of a tiny editor facing an enormous programmable environment. Vim developed scripting, plugins, and a growing collection of features. Describing modern Vim as though it were the original vi confuses an inherited editing style with an unchanged implementation. The names in the argument evolved along with the software.
Why Emacs vs Vim still comes up

The remaining disagreement often concerns where someone wants to spend their working day. Some people want an extensible environment organized around Emacs. Others want Vim's modal commands wherever they edit. A preference can survive changes in hardware because the learned motions still feel comfortable, even after the original resource constraints have disappeared.

There is no requirement to choose every part of one tradition. Evil provides a vi layer inside Emacs and emulates Vim's main features. Its existence is a useful answer to the claim that modal editing and an extensible Emacs environment are fundamentally incompatible. Users can choose the editing commands and the surrounding environment separately.

source.label: Evil documentation: Vim editing inside Emacs.

blocks.text: For anyone tracing the rivalry, the dates worth remembering are the 1970s origins, the visible disputes of the 1980s, and Vim's arrival in 1991. The evidence supports a rivalry that accumulated through use, argument, and imitation. It does not support a single founding confrontation. The interesting question is how two ways of editing became habits that programmers wanted everyone else to share.

hero.alt: Two vintage terminals show branching functions and compact editing commands, representing Emacs and vi.
hero.text: Emacs and vi grew from different editing traditions. Conceptual AI-generated illustration.

posts.title: SCO Unix and AT&T: From Bell Labs to Court
posts.description: Trace SCO Unix from AT&T Bell Labs and Microsoft Xenix to OpenServer, Novell, Caldera, and the Linux lawsuits. A history of the companies and disputed rights.

hero.alt: A minicomputer, business server, connected terminals, and contract binders represent stages in Unix history.
hero.text: From Bell Labs research to business servers and disputed contracts. Conceptual AI-generated illustration.

blocks.text: WARNING: HISTORY LESSON

The history of SCO Unix begins with AT&T's Bell Labs, where Unix emerged in 1969. The Santa Cruz Operation later helped turn that research operating system into software businesses could run on Intel computers. A different company, eventually called The SCO Group, acquired the Unix business and became known for lawsuits involving Linux. Confusing those companies makes almost every subsequent event harder to understand.

Three things traveled through this history on different terms: software, contractual rights, and the UNIX trademark. A company could sell a Unix product without owning every copyright behind it. A system could behave like Unix without containing AT&T code. A transfer of business assets could leave important rights with the seller. Those distinctions became expensive questions in court, but they also explain how Unix spread.
1969: Unix begins inside Bell Labs

Unix started after Bell Labs withdrew from Multics, an ambitious shared computing project. Ken Thompson wanted an environment in which he could continue programming. Working with colleagues including Dennis Ritchie, he developed a smaller system on a PDP-7. Ritchie's retrospective describes experimentation with a filesystem, processes, and tools, rather than a corporate plan to conquer the operating system market.

source.label: Dennis Ritchie on the evolution of Unix.

blocks.text: The early machines were scarce resources. Sharing one computer among several people meant managing files, running programs, and keeping users from accidentally interfering with one another. Unix supplied those services through a relatively small collection of mechanisms. Its command interpreter, the shell, was a program users could replace, rather than an inseparable part of the kernel.

Thompson and Ritchie's 1974 paper describes a system used for programming and document preparation, including patent applications. That last detail matters. Unix was already doing useful office work while its creators refined it. The paper explains how programs could communicate through pipes, allowing the output of one command to become another command's input.

source.label: Thompson and Ritchie's original Unix paper (PDF).

blocks.text: A pipe turns several small operations into a larger task.

One command might select records, another sort them, and another count them. The user supplies the arrangement. This approach encouraged people to write reusable tools, since a program did not need to anticipate every possible report someone might request. Much of the familiar Unix working style grew around that possibility.

The rewrite in C during 1973 made the system less dependent on one machine's assembly language. Portability still required substantial engineering. Ritchie's history of C describes later work moving Unix to other hardware, including the Interdata effort. The important change was that moving the operating system became a tractable project, rather than necessarily starting again from scratch.

source.label: Ritchie on C and the work of portability (PDF).

blocks.alt: A vintage research computer room contains a minicomputer, terminal, printer, and open notebooks.
blocks.text: Unix began as a research computing environment. Conceptual AI-generated illustration, not an archival photograph.
How AT&T Unix reached universities and vendors

AT&T licensed Unix outside Bell Labs. Universities could obtain source code under relatively inexpensive academic arrangements, while commercial licensing followed different terms. Access to the source allowed researchers to study how the system worked and change it. It did not place the software in the public domain or grant the freedoms associated with later open source licenses.

source.label: Bell Labs on Unix licensing and academic distribution.

blocks.text: Berkeley became an important center of Unix development. Its distributions added software and improvements, eventually including networking work supported by DARPA. For part of that history, Berkeley distributions still depended on licensed AT&T material. Describing every historical BSD release as freely redistributable would erase the licensing conditions under which many early users received it.

Think of source access as permission to inspect the machinery under specified conditions. It answers one question about a program, but not every question about copying, selling, or redistributing it. That distinction is easy to miss when reading the history backward from today's public repositories. Researchers sharing improvements were working within a legal arrangement as well as a technical community.

AT&T developed its commercial Unix line alongside these outside efforts. System V appeared in 1983 and became a reference point for vendors selling their own implementations. The family names matter because Unix never settled into one product with one release schedule. A customer might encounter research editions, Berkeley software, or a vendor's System V derivative, each carrying different additions and support arrangements.

source.label: Bell Labs' timeline of Unix versions.

blocks.text: The resulting variety was useful and troublesome. Vendors could adapt an operating system to their machines and customers. Developers then had to determine which features an application could safely expect. A familiar shell prompt did not guarantee identical libraries, administration commands, or binary formats. Compatibility became something businesses purchased, tested, and negotiated, rather than something the name alone could promise.
Microsoft Xenix and the original Santa Cruz Operation

Microsoft announced Xenix in August 1980 as a portable Unix-based operating system. This surprises readers who know the company chiefly through DOS and Windows. At the time, licensing software for different computer manufacturers was an important part of its business. Xenix belonged to that period, when the future shape of the personal computer market remained unsettled.

source.label: Microsoft's history of its 1980 Xenix announcement.

blocks.text: The Santa Cruz Operation, founded in 1979 by Doug Michels and Larry Michels, worked on Unix ports and related development. Its own company history records packaged Xenix products for Intel machines in 1983, followed by versions for the 286 and 386. That history is a company retrospective, useful for its product sequence but best read without adopting its promotional superlatives.

source.label: Archived Santa Cruz Operation company history.

blocks.text: SCO's achievement was commercial as much as technical.

A working operating system needed installation procedures, drivers, documentation, application suppliers, and someone customers could call. The company built relationships with resellers and software developers. These businesses could deliver a complete installation instead of leaving the buyer to assemble a research system and solve every compatibility problem independently.

Imagine a small wholesaler choosing a computer system. Several employees need inventory, invoices, and customer records at the same time. A central computer connected to terminals offers one place to store the data and run the application. The sale includes the accounting package, installation, training, and maintenance. The operating system matters because it makes that arrangement work reliably. A terminal in this arrangement was not necessarily a separate computer running its own copy of the business application. It could provide a keyboard and screen connected to the central machine. Multiple sessions shared that machine's processor, disks, and installed software. Adding a desk therefore did not automatically require another full application installation. The same arrangement also concentrated responsibility for backups and availability on the server.

This hypothetical customer helps explain the market without pretending every installation was identical. The buyer might care little about the history of Bell Labs. The person responsible for payroll would care greatly if an upgrade broke the application. A reseller who understood the customer's printer, backup routine, and software could therefore matter more than a new feature in the kernel.

blocks.alt: An office server connects three terminal desks beside a printer and stocked shelves.
blocks.text: A central server could support several employees using a business application. Conceptual AI-generated illustration.
SCO Unix and OpenServer become business products

SCO released its System V/386 Unix product in 1989. The OpenServer family followed in 1992. These names describe product development by the original Santa Cruz Operation, well before the later SCO Group's litigation campaign. The company also sold applications and networking components around its operating systems, making the complete business environment part of the purchase.

source.label: SCO's chronology of Unix and OpenServer products.

blocks.text: The shift from earlier Intel processors to the 386 widened what a PC-based Unix system could support. But a faster processor was only one part of a successful upgrade. Applications had to run, peripherals needed drivers, and administrators needed procedures they trusted. Selling a server meant supporting the combination, not simply demonstrating that the operating system could boot.

Consider the cost of replacing a working order-entry system. Someone must move the records, verify calculations, reconnect printers, train employees, and arrange a fallback if the migration fails. Even when another operating system costs less, that project consumes time and carries risk. This is why an installed application can remain valuable after its underlying platform stops attracting much attention.

There was another compatibility distinction: source compatibility versus binary compatibility. Developers might be able to rebuild a program for a new system while customers could not run their existing executable unchanged. If a supplier had disappeared, obtaining source code or a replacement build could become difficult. An apparently straightforward operating system replacement could then depend on rights, documentation, and people outside the customer's control. It also explains why accounts of computing history centered on enthusiasts can miss commercial Unix. New desktops and developer tools leave abundant public discussion. A server processing invoices in a back room may leave almost none. Lack of fashionable attention tells us little about how important the machine was to the business that depended on it.
AT&T, Novell, and the 1995 Unix transaction

AT&T placed its Unix business in Unix System Laboratories, or USL. Outside investors joined USL in 1991. Novell announced its planned acquisition in 1992 and completed it in 1993. The change put a major commercial Unix business inside a company associated with network software, at a time when vendors were competing to define the server market.

source.label: Bell Labs on USL and Novell's acquisition.

blocks.text: Standards organizations were another part of this story. X/Open worked to specify interfaces that applications could rely on across vendors. Stewardship of the UNIX trademark moved to X/Open during the 1993–1994 period, and The Open Group later continued the certification program. Trademark certification and ownership of historical source code were separate matters.

source.label: The Open Group's Unix history and standards timeline.

blocks.text: The industry also divided over competing alliances. AT&T and Sun announced cooperation in 1987, and rival vendors formed the Open Software Foundation in response. These disputes helped give the period its Unix wars label. They concerned influence over the platform as well as technical choices. Customers and application developers had reasons to want common interfaces even when vendors preferred their own commercial strategies.

source.label: The Open Group on competing Unix alliances.

blocks.text: A trademark identifies a product under particular rules. Copyright concerns protected expression, including software code. A license grants permissions, which may be limited by contracts. These categories can overlap in a commercial deal, but they do not become interchangeable. Reading an announcement that a company bought a Unix business tells us less than reading the agreement that defined the assets.

That mattered greatly after Novell and Santa Cruz signed their 1995 asset purchase agreement. The transaction transferred a Unix business, including UnixWare, but its treatment of copyrights and retained contractual powers became disputed. An amendment followed in 1996. Years later, courts had to interpret the agreement and amendment together, rather than treating the purchase as a simple transfer of everything called Unix.

source.label: The appellate court's account of the asset purchase agreement (PDF).

blocks.alt: Source listings and disks sit in an archive box beside a separate contracts folder and key.
blocks.text: Source code, contractual rights, and trademark stewardship followed different paths. Conceptual AI-generated illustration.

For a reader following the companies, the safest habit is to keep separate columns: who sells the product, who administers the contracts, who owns the disputed code, and who controls certification. The names in those columns need not match. Much of the later confusion came from collapsing them into one question about who owned Unix.
Why GNU and Linux changed the competition

Richard Stallman announced GNU in September 1983 as a project to build a complete Unix-compatible software system that users could freely share. His announcement listed an editor, compiler, shell, and other components alongside a kernel. This was a plan to implement a familiar computing environment under different terms, not an offer to redistribute AT&T's existing source code.

Linux supplied another independently developed part of that environment. Linus Torvalds began the kernel in 1991, and other programmers contributed over the network. The kernel project's description emphasizes both its Unix-like behavior and its implementation from scratch. It also distinguishes the kernel from a distribution, which packages the additional software needed for a usable system.

source.label: The Linux kernel project's explanation of Linux.

blocks.text: GNU's account describes how its tools and the Linux kernel could form a complete operating system. This offered a route to Unix-style computing outside the traditional proprietary vendor arrangement. It did not eliminate the need for integration, testing, or support. Those jobs could be supplied by a distribution vendor, a consultant, or an organization's own administrators.

source.label: GNU's account of the combined system.

blocks.text: For an established Unix supplier, that changed the comparison a customer could make. The customer could consider retaining familiar commands while buying support differently. An application still needed compatible interfaces, suitable libraries, and a tested migration path. Familiarity reduced some switching costs without removing them all. That tension helps explain why commercial Unix products and Linux distributions could compete for new installations while older systems continued operating.
Project Monterey and the Caldera purchase

In 1999, IBM described Project Monterey as a collaboration involving IBM, SCO, and Sequent, with Intel participating. The proposal combined technologies associated with AIX, UnixWare, and DYNIX/ptx across several processor families. It was an attempt to give commercial Unix a stronger shared direction while preserving the capabilities and customers of the participating vendors.

The brochure is evidence of what the companies proposed, not proof that every promised product appeared. That distinction matters when reading technology announcements. A plan can reveal competitive pressures and engineering ambitions while telling us little about what customers ultimately installed. Monterey also places SCO in an industry of partnerships, shared development, and contracts that later became subjects of dispute.

Caldera completed its acquisition of SCO's server and professional services businesses in May 2001. The announcement included the OpenServer and UnixWare product lines and promoted a combination of Unix experience with Linux opportunities. The original Santa Cruz company continued around its Tarantella business. Caldera acquired the Unix operation, rather than turning every part of the old company into a new one.

source.label: Caldera's May 2001 acquisition announcement, reproduced by LWN.

blocks.text: This is the break in the family tree that abbreviated histories often skip.

The familiar SCO name later belonged to the buyer. People could encounter the same product names and recognize the same initials while the corporate identity had changed. Following the operating systems alone would therefore produce a different timeline from following the legal entities.

Caldera began using the SCO Group identity in 2002. Its SEC filings record shareholder approval of the formal corporate name change in May 2003. The distinction between branding and the legal name explains why histories give different dates for the change. Neither date means that the original Santa Cruz Operation was founded again.

source.label: SCO Group's SEC account of its corporate history.

blocks.text: The SCO Group, IBM, and the Linux allegations

In 2003, The SCO Group sued IBM. The dispute involved contractual obligations and alleged misuse of Unix-related material in connection with Linux. SCO also pursued licensing revenue through its SCOsource program. Its filings describe those claims from the company's perspective. They should be read as statements of its position, not independent findings that Linux infringed its rights.

source.label: SCO Group's disclosures about litigation and SCOsource.

blocks.text: The allegations attracted attention because they challenged assumptions behind a rapidly spreading operating system. But technical resemblance alone cannot establish the copying of protected code. A filesystem, shell, or programming interface may follow familiar conventions without being the same implementation. To assess a particular accusation, one needs the identified material, its history, and the rights attached to it.

It helps to separate four questions. What code or conduct was challenged? Which agreement or legal right supposedly covered it? Who possessed that right? Which issues did the court decide? Reporting that skips one of these steps can turn an accusation about specified material into an unsupported claim about an entire operating system.
The IBM litigation and the Novell dispute were related but distinct proceedings.

The former concerned IBM's conduct and contractual issues. The latter addressed ownership and powers flowing from the Novell transaction. A ruling in one could affect the assumptions behind the other without deciding every claim. Treating them as a single lawsuit obscures both the chronology and the legal reasoning.

blocks.alt: Legal folders, a technical manual, and a terminal appear in front of a courthouse silhouette.
blocks.text: The lawsuits required courts to examine specific contracts and rights. Conceptual AI-generated illustration.
Bankruptcy and the Unix copyright verdict

SCO filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on September 14, 2007. Its contemporaneous SEC notice supplies the date directly. Bankruptcy added another set of proceedings involving the company's assets and obligations, alongside the litigation already underway. The continued existence of a product business and the financial condition of its owner were separate questions.

In March 2010, a Utah jury found that Novell owned the Unix and UnixWare copyrights at issue. Novell announced the verdict immediately. The wording matters: this was a decision about the disputed historical copyrights, not a declaration that Novell owned every Unix-related program or every operating system with Unix-like behavior.

source.label: Novell's announcement of the 2010 jury verdict.

blocks.text: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the judgment in 2011. Its opinion also addressed Novell's retained authority concerning certain license agreements. That outcome defeated the claim that the disputed copyrights had transferred through the transaction as SCO asserted. It did not, by itself, close every separate dispute associated with SCO, IBM, or later owners of the operating system products.

A useful history must resist rewriting earlier events as though this result had always been obvious. The parties disputed contract language, offered competing interpretations, and litigated through several stages. At the same time, uncertainty during a lawsuit is no reason to preserve an allegation as fact after the relevant judgment. The record changes what a responsible account can say.
What survived the SCO Unix disputes

UnXis announced completion of its purchase of the SCO Unix operating system assets in April 2011. The product business continued beyond the bankrupt company's most familiar public identity. This was another asset transaction, so it should not be mistaken for a court ruling or a fresh transfer of every right ever associated with Unix.

source.label: UnXis announces its 2011 purchase of operating system assets.

blocks.text: Xinuos, the business later associated with those products, continues to list OpenServer and UnixWare offerings. Their survival makes an important historical point. A platform can disappear from mainstream conversation while remaining relevant to customers with established applications. Product maintenance, migration decisions, and courtroom headlines operate on different schedules.

source.label: Xinuos and its continuing operating system products.

blocks.text: SCO's history therefore has more than one ending.

The original company helped businesses buy Unix on comparatively accessible hardware. Caldera acquired that operation and adopted its name. The SCO Group then pursued claims whose central copyright premise failed in court. Customers, meanwhile, still had software to run and records to preserve.

The wider Unix tradition also survived these corporate changes. Its tools, interfaces, and working habits spread well beyond any single vendor. The editor arguments discussed in my history of Emacs and Vim belong to that broader culture, where people carried learned habits from one system to another even when the machine and supplier changed.

source.label: Related: how the Emacs and Vim rivalry began.

blocks.text: When someone says SCO bought Unix from AT&T, ask which company, which transaction, and which rights they mean. The intervening names matter: USL, Novell, Santa Cruz, and Caldera. Following those details reveals how a research system became a commercial product, how customers kept it useful, and why a short ownership slogan could never explain the resulting history.
